title: A voice for each character in a play
statement: Whether giving each character in a play read aloud its own voice helps learners track who is speaking is untested.
detail: A review of a Grade 9 prototype warns that the argument that distinct voices reduce the load of tracking who is speaking in a play is reasoning, not a cited finding, that there is no evidence specifically on multi-voice drama read aloud, and that it should not be presented as evidence-based. The same review notes that actor-read audio brings different voices with the casting, so nothing would need building for it.

evidence.quote: The argument that distinct voices reduce the load of tracking who is speaking in a play is reasoning, not a cited finding. There is no evidence specifically on multi-voice drama read-aloud.
It should not be presented as evidence-based.
If the audio is actor-read, that is not a feature to build — it comes with the casting.
The argument that distinct voices reduce the load of tracking who is speaking in a play is reasoning, not a cited finding. There is no evidence specifically on multi-voice drama read-aloud.
That literature is about prose, where speaker attribution is not a problem, so the general null does not straightforwardly transfer to multi-voice drama.
The reading-while-listening literature gives a small overall benefit (g ≈ 0.18) which is largely a pacing artifact
